This is robot. Late 1960s to 1970s.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The robot dance evolved from early 20th-century mime acts that imitated mechanical figures.
In the late 1960s, it transitioned into social dance in American funk and soul clubs, pioneered by Charles "Robot" Washington and "Robot Ann" who danced it socially to music.
Michael Jackson popularized the dance globally in 1973 with televised performances of "Dancing Machine".
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally part of theatrical mime and social dancing at funk and soul parties, the robot became a performance dance symbolizing mechanical and futuristic themes.
It is performed socially, in competitions, on television, and in popular media.
The dance is not sacred or restricted.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers maintain a rigid, mechanical posture, moving limbs in segmented, stilted motions.
Each movement begins and ends with a dimestop—an abrupt halt simulating a motor starting or stopping.
The dance can be performed solo or socially, with or without music.
Watch for Dimestop.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (wt_nbTRzYrk)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Performed solo, socially in couples, or in small groups; spatial paths are linear or angular to simulate mechanical motion.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The robot is often danced to music with clear, steady beats such as electrofunk, which enhances the mechanical illusion.
Music with a 'robot theme' is also common, even if not rhythmically ideal.
Listen for the synthesizer, drum machine, bass guitar.
Electronic funk with steady, repetitive beats, synthesizer melodies, and rhythmic bass lines that emphasize clear downbeats to match the robot's mechanical stops.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 — First steps. Today: Master basic isolated limb movements and dimestops..
Level: Beginner. Difficulty of the dance overall: beginner to intermediate.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Rigid, upright, with controlled muscle tension to simulate mechanical stiffness.
Segmented, isolated arm movements with abrupt stops (dimestops). Hands often held stiffly, mimicking robot joints.
Minimal movement; torso remains stiff to maintain robotic illusion.
on_screen: Instructor front then side view; freeze-frame on validated posture

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stand upright with a rigid posture.
Step 2: Isolate one arm and move it slowly in a segmented motion.
Drill: Practice slow arm movements with abrupt stops.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Perform a dimestop by abruptly halting the arm movement.
Step 4: Repeat with the other arm and legs, maintaining mechanical stiffness.
Drill: Isolate leg movements with clear starts and stops.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Combine arm and leg movements maintaining rigidity.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Loose or fluid movements that break the mechanical illusion.
Teachers of this dance warn against: moving everything below the elbow instead of including the elbow
Teachers of this dance warn against: not maintaining enough tension in the movements
Teachers of this dance warn against: not coordinating the head and body movements
